The album was initially planned to be more "energetic" than his previous work, but ended up presenting a wide range of styles such as [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B), [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music), [reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music), [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk) and [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music). Lyrically, Unorthodox Jukebox revolves around the theme of relationships, incorporating more explicit lyrics and subjects than his previous material. Critical response to Unorthodox Jukebox was generally favorable; many [reviewers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_journalism) compared Mars's work to that of his previous album, while others deemed its lyrics shallow.

It debuted at number two on the US [Billboard 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200), with first week sales of 192,000 copies, and later topped the chart. The record also reached number one in Australia, Canada, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. The album was certified six-times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America) (RIAA), eight times platinum by both the [Recorded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recorded_Music_NZ)

**Unorthodox Jukebox** is the second studio album by the American singer and songwriter [Bruno Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_Mars). It was released on December 7, 2012, by [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records) and was made available to listen to in its entirety for a week before its release. It serves as the follow-up to Mars's debut record [Doo-Wops & Hooligans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doo-Wops_&_Hooligans) (2010). Mars's writing and production team, [the Smeezingtons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Smeezingtons), composed the whole record and worked with several past collaborators, [Jeff Bhasker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Bhasker) and [Supa Dups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supa_Dups), while enlisting new producers, such as [Mark Ronson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Ronson) and [Emile Haynie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emile_Haynie).

Unorthodox Jukebox was the fourth best-selling album in 2013 and it has since sold six million units globally as of 2016. In 2014, Unorthodox Jukebox won the [Grammy Award for Best Pop Vocal Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Pop_Vocal_Album) at the [56th Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/56th_Annual_Grammy_Awards) and [International Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juno_Award_for_International_Album_of_the_Year) at the [Juno Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juno_Awards).

Unorthodox Jukebox was supported by five singles, including two US [Billboard Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100) number ones "[Locked Out of Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locked_Out_of_Heaven)" and "[When I Was Your Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_I_Was_Your_Man)", which also experienced commercial acclaim in various countries, with the former also topping the [Canadian Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Hot_100). Subsequently, three other [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_%28music%29) ("[Treasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasure_%28song%29)", "[Gorilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorilla_%28song%29)", and "[Young Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Girls)") were made

Background [\[ edit \]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unorthodox_Jukebox&action=edit&section=1)
Conception [\[ edit \]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unorthodox_Jukebox&action=edit&section=2)

After ending [The Doo-Wops & Hooligans Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doo-Wops_&_Hooligans_Tour), [Bruno Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_Mars) implied that he was going to take some time creating and perfecting his second full-length album. He additionally confessed that, "It's going to come when it comes" since his production team, [the Smeezingtons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Smeezingtons), felt that they rushed his debut album because of the release's deadline. "We just want it to be perfect", the singer added.<sup>[1]</sup> Due to the numerous television shows and worldwide performances provided by Mars, he acknowledged that his second studio album needed to display his "raucously" dynamic appearances on stage.<sup>[2]</sup>

Mars revealed to [Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_%28magazine%29) in September 2012 on a preview of his cover story that he recorded an album that represented his freedom.<sup>[3]</sup> On his debut record, [Doo-Wops & Hooligans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doo-Wops_&_Hooligans), the singer reportedly had to change some things because of pressure from his label, something he was displeased with.<sup>[2]</sup> He clarified that Unorthodox Jukebox was more of him and what he stands for, mainly because he didn't have to modify things. He elaborated, "If I'm changing things around because people might think it's a hard pill to swallow then I'm going to feel like a circus clown onstage, selling something fake".<sup>[2]</sup> The variety of music styles presented on Unorthodox Jukebox resulted in his rejection from his label several times in the past; he also confessed that he had to face criticism by label presidents, who—according to him—expressed, "Your music sucks, you don't know who you are, your music is all over the place, and we don't know how to market this stuff. Pick a lane and come back to us". To these statements, the singer added that he felt "disgusted" as he wanted to have the liberty to create his own music and not the music he was told to do.<sup>[2]</sup>

have worked on the album.<sup>[3][9]</sup> The first song written for Unorthodox Jukebox was "[Gorilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorilla_%28song%29)", which "set the tone for the entire project"; Mars explained in an interview granted to [MTV News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_News) that it became its mascot hence the reason it ended up as the album cover.<sup>[10]</sup> In an interview for the [Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone), Blanco confessed, "I got a really cool song with him. Me and Paul [Epworth] just got together and Bruno wrote an amazing song on top of it. It kind of all came together". He further explained that "it's like some throwback [Nina Simone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nina_Simone) type shit, like 'Sinnerman'". Additionally, a "pianolaced" track was conceived for the album in its opening session.<sup>[9]</sup>

blocks.content: Mars explained the meaning behind the album's title by saying that it had become a "soulful, experimental, electronic, hard-to-explain" concept.<sup>[6]</sup> In

order to record an album like that, it was—according to him—mandatory to experiment and not follow any known pattern, resulting the guests enlisted for the record to be unexpected. According to the singer, jazz artist [Esperanza Spalding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanza_Spalding) and Diplo were among them. Furthermore, the "pop's most innovative producers" (Bhasker, Haynie and Ronson) had to be taken "beyond their comfort zone".<sup>[6]</sup> While being interviewed for his Billboard Artist of the Year cover story, Mars complimented Ronson and Bhasker by explaining that "it's not about what's hot on the radio or the fastest way to make a buck, these guys are fearless, doing the music they want to do".<sup>[4]</sup> Mars additionally felt that "when there are no safe bets, that's when [he feels his] blood move."<sup>[6]</sup>

Mars also worked with [Michael Leonhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Leonhart) on three songs for the album, including on an unreleased version of "[Locked Out of Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locked_Out_of_Heaven)".<sup>[11]</sup> By the end of September 2012, the singer was reportedly "fine-tuning" the mixing of a track until 5 a.m. with Manny Marroquin, mainly because of his disappointment with "[It Will Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It_Will_Rain)"'s final mix.<sup>[2][3]</sup> Starting with mid-October, the Smeezingtons were making the final touches on the album at Levcon Studios (their studio); Ari Levine sent a few tracks over e-mail with their final mixes to Mars, who was still in Manhattan after hosting [Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live).<sup>[8]</sup>
Composition [\[ edit \]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unorthodox_Jukebox&action=edit&section=4)

Unorthodox Jukebox is a pop, R&B, rock, [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk), soul, [reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae) and [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco) r<sub>ecord</sub>.[12][13][14] The album opens with "[Young Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Girls)", a [midtempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo) pop ballad which deals with the idea of indulging in the dubious charms of young girls, even though the singer recognizes that what he is doing is wrong.<sup>[4][15]</sup> The song was reregistered in [ASCAP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Society_of_Composers,_Authors_and_Publishers) with a new writing credit by [Mac Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_Davis).<sup>[16]</sup> "Locked Out of Heaven", a [reggae rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae_rock) and [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock) track that incorporates elements of [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music) and funk, is the subsequent track and the [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single).<sup>[12][17][18]</sup> Musically, it contains booming synthesizers, a [four-on-the-floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_on_the_floor_%28music%29) chorus, while lyrically exploring themes of love.<sup>[19][20]</sup> Comparisons were established between "Locked Out of Heaven" and the rock/reggae style used by English band [The Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Police).<sup>[19][21][22]</sup> "Gorilla" was described by Mars as being about "good old animalistic sex".<sup>[8]</sup> The track portrays a midtempo rock and [soft rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_rock) song,<sup>[4][23]</sup> while lyrically expressing male [chauvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chauvinism) sentiments<sup>[24]</sup> and making reference to his 2010 arrest for [cocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine) possession.<sup>[25]</sup> "[Treasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasure_%28song%29)", the album's third single, is a [disco-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco-pop) song, inspired by English duo [Wham!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wham!) and

position for six weeks, marking Mars's longest-running number-one on the chart after previously released "[Just the Way You Are](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_the_Way_You_Are_%28Bruno_Mars_song%29)" (2010) and "[Grenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenade_%28song%29)" (2010) each topped the chart for four editions.<sup>[40]</sup> The song further peaked at number one in Canada and on the US [Pop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainstream_Top_40) chart, while reaching the top ten in more than twenty countries.<sup>[41][42]</sup>

"When I Was Your Man" was released on January 15, 2013, as the album's second single.<sup>[43]</sup> It had previously been premiered as the album's third and final [promotional single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promotional_single) one month and a half prior to its stand-alone release.<sup>[44]</sup> The track was critically acclaimed, receiving praising for being an "emotional ballad" and for featuring a "minimal musical accompaniment".<sup>[44][45]</sup> The song topped the Billboard Hot 100 chart, becoming the singer's fifth number one single in the United States and it reached the top fifteen in several fellow territories.<sup>[46][47]</sup> "When I Was Your Man" was nominated for [Best Pop Solo Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Pop_Solo_Performance) at the [56th Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/56th_Annual_Grammy_Awards).<sup>[48]</sup>

"Treasure" was subsequently confirmed as the record's third single by [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records).<sup>[49]</sup> It received generally favorable reviews from critics, who praised it for "[echoing] the peppy sound of such pop/R&B hitmakers of the 1970s and 1980s as [the Sylvers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sylvers), [Heatwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heatwave_%28band%29), [DeBarge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeBarge) and [Kool & the Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kool_&_the_Gang)."<sup>[50]</sup> To promote the single, Mars performed on various occasions, including a "little extra Michael Jackson-esque, circa [Off the Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off_the_Wall) and [Thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_%28album%29)" show at the 2013 [Billboard Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Music_Award).<sup>[51]</sup> Commercially, "Treasure" reached the top five in the United States and other eighteen countries.<sup>[41][52]</sup>

"Gorilla", confirmed as the next single for Unorthodox Jukebox,<sup>[53]</sup> was produced by the Smeezingtons, Mark Ronson, Jeff Bhasker and Emile Haynie, who previously handled the process for the record's lead single.<sup>[7]</sup> The track impacted American [pop radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio) on September 10, 2013, thus peaking at number 22 on the Billboard Hot 100 and becoming the singer's first single not to reach the top ten there.<sup>[41][54]</sup> Mars performed the single for the first time during the [2013 MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_MTV_Video_Music_Awards).<sup>[53]</sup>

"Young Girls" was released as the fifth and final single from the album. Mars announced its availability during an interview with [Nova 96.9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_96.9), an Australian radio station, on November 26, 2013.<sup>[55]</sup> Commercially, its charting was influenced by its stand-alone release as the record's first promotional single on November 6, 2012, through [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store).<sup>[56]</sup> Unmaterialized plans for a music video to accompany "Young Girls" were made in 2012.<sup>[10]</sup>
Release and promotion [\[ edit \]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unorthodox_Jukebox&action=edit&section=6)
See also: [The Moonshine Jungle Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Moonshine_Jungle_Tour)

On September 4, 2012, Mars reported to his fanbase that, "You'll hear something in October. I promise", after being asked for news regarding his second studio album.<sup>[57]</sup> On September 19, 2012, the singer announced the release of Unorthodox Jukebox via [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) after having worked on it for a year. He further posted a link to a "Funny or Die" video entitled "Whatta Man", where Mars starred himself in order to celebrate.<sup>[58]</sup> On September 28, 2012, Billboard

2025, Unorthodox Jukebox was certified eight times platinum in New Zealand.<sup>[124]</sup> The record entered the Australian charts at number three, gradually climbing to the top spot, with it bringing total sales to 210,000 units and being similarly certified by the [Australian Recording Industry Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Recording_Industry_Association) (ARIA).<sup>[125][126]</sup> It was the third best-selling album in Australia in 2013.<sup>[127]</sup> In Canada, Unorthodox Jukebox opened the [Canadian Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Albums_Chart) at number two, later reaching number one on the week ending July 20, 2013.<sup>[128][129]</sup> It was certified eight times platinum by [Music Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Canada) (MC).<sup>[130]</sup> In Japan, the album debuted at number eleven on the [Oricon Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oricon).<sup>[131]</sup> In mid-year 2017, the record sold a total of 250,000 units, therefore reaching platinum status.<sup>[132]</sup> In 2014, the album topped the [Mexican Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asociaci%C3%B3n_Mexicana_de_Productores_de_Fonogramas_y_Videogramas) and remains the ninth best-selling release there, with it spending 106 weeks in the chart.<sup>[133]</sup> It also earned a two times platinum+gold certification for exceeding sales of over 150,000 copies in that territory.<sup>[134]</sup> As of 2014, Unorthodox Jukebox sold 3.2 million units globally,<sup>[135]</sup> while bringing totals sales to six million copies by March 2016.<sup>[136]</sup>
